subject: History
title: Mesopotamia
learningOutcomes: Differentiate between primary and secondary sources of history and explain why we study human history.
Define civilization and analyse the components that let a society move from nomadic life to organized urban centers.
Evaluate the importance of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in sustaining agriculture in the Fertile Crescent.
Analyse the social order, religious beliefs, family life, and eventual decline of the Sumer Valley civilization.
Describe the innovations of the ancient Mesopotamians, including cuneiform writing, the wheel, and architecture.
Analyse the Babylonian Empire and the impact of the Code of Hammurabi and rulers such as Sargon and Nebuchadnezzar II.

sections.heading: Why We Study History
sections.body: People study history to understand the past and make sense of the present world. The events of the past shape today's cultures, borders, governments, and ways of life. By studying the patterns of cause and effect in history, it becomes possible to recognise how events unfold and even to predict what may happen in the future.

sections.heading: Prehistory, Timelines, and Eras
sections.body: Prehistory is the period of human history before written records. We learn about it mainly through archaeological discoveries, study, and research. A timeline is a chronological sequence of events shown along a drawn line with dates. The past is also divided into large stretches of time called ages, eras, or periods, each usually covering more than one century.

sections.heading: What Is a Civilization?
sections.body: A civilization is the society, culture, and way of life of people living in a certain area at a specific time, including their beliefs, governance, art, architecture, and law. Most civilizations began near rivers, which provided water and fertile alluvial soil deposited by floods. This surplus of food let populations grow and civilizations expand into neighbouring areas.

sections.heading: The Four River Valley Civilizations
sections.body: The four major river valley civilizations were Mesopotamia (between the Tigris and Euphrates), Ancient Egypt (along the Nile), the Indus Valley (along the Indus), and the Chinese civilization (along the Yellow River). Dates are counted in BCE (Before Common Era) and CE (Common Era). The Mesopotamian civilization flourished from roughly 6000 BCE to 2500 BCE, making it one of the oldest.

sections.heading: The Six Components of a Civilization
sections.body: Historians identify six key components of a civilization: urban centers, government, social order, beliefs, art, and writing. Urban centers need a surplus food supply so people can take up other professions. Government rules and defends the territory, social order divides society into classes, beliefs guide daily life, art preserves a civilization's legacy, and writing records knowledge and law.

sections.heading: Mesopotamia and the Fertile Crescent
sections.body: Mesopotamia is Greek for 'land between two rivers'. It lay within the Fertile Crescent, a crescent-shaped region between the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean Sea, mainly in modern-day Iraq. Because writing, laws, cities, and agriculture first developed together here, Mesopotamia is called the cradle of civilization.

sections.heading: The Rivers Tigris and Euphrates
sections.body: The Tigris and Euphrates rose in the highlands of present-day Türkiye and flowed south-east into the Persian Gulf. Their regular floods left fertile silt, and Mesopotamians dug canals to irrigate their fields, growing wheat and barley. As irrigation improved, villages grew rapidly into cities, and several civilizations — Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians — mushroomed near each other.

sections.heading: Sumer: Society, Beliefs, and Innovations
sections.body: Sumer lay in the southern-most part of Mesopotamia. Its society had four classes: nobles, commoners, clients, and slaves. Every city had a Ziggurat, its temple and administrative centre. The Sumerians were polytheists who saw their gods as anthropomorphic yet immortal. Facing floods, droughts, and hostile neighbours, they dug irrigation canals, built mud-and-brick walls, and used barter trade for materials.

sections.heading: Writing, Family Life, and the Decline of Sumer
sections.body: The Sumerians invented cuneiform, the world's first writing system, made of wedge-shaped symbols on clay tablets. The Epic of Gilgamesh, written around 2000 BCE, was translated by George Smith in 1872 CE. The family was the basic social unit. Because the Sumerian city states were constantly at war and never unified, they were defeated by the Akkadians around 2300 BCE and later by the Babylonians.

sections.heading: The Babylonians, Famous Rulers, and Sources of History
sections.body: The Babylonians built on Sumerian achievements, giving the world the wheel, the plough, the sundial clock, the 24-hour day, the 60-minute hour, the 12-month calendar, and the first recorded laws. Sargon (2334–2279 BCE) founded the Akkadian Empire; Nebuchadnezzar II (604–562 BCE) built the Hanging Gardens; and Hammurabi (1792–1750 BCE) inscribed his Code of 282 laws. Historians reconstruct all this from primary sources (artefacts, ruins) and secondary sources (textbooks, biographies).

definitions.definition: The period of human history before written records existed.
The society, culture, and way of life of a group of people in a specific area and time.
Fertile soil deposited by floodwaters, very good for farming.
A crescent-shaped region in the Middle East known for its fertile land.
Greek for 'land between two rivers', the region between the Tigris and Euphrates.
The region where human civilization is believed to have first started.
The ancient Mesopotamian temple, the most important building in each Sumerian city.
The highest social class, wealthy people who owned large estates.
People who believe in and worship more than one god.
Having a human form, shape, or characteristics.
Trading goods directly for other goods without using money.
The ancient Sumerian writing system made of wedge-shaped symbols pressed into clay.
A single large stone, sometimes used for writing or as a monument.
The empire founded by King Sargon that united much of Mesopotamia around 2334 BCE.
The second major Babylonian Empire (626–539 BCE), at its peak under Nebuchadnezzar II.
The world's first written set of laws, created by King Hammurabi, containing 282 laws.
An original, first-hand record from the time being studied.
An account written by someone who was not present at the time.

examTips: Remember the meaning of Mesopotamia — Greek for 'land between two rivers' (the Tigris and Euphrates).
Learn the six components of a civilization in order: urban centers, government, social order, beliefs, art, writing.
Know the four Sumerian social classes top to bottom: nobles, commoners, clients, slaves.
Match each ruler to a headline fact: Sargon → Akkadian Empire; Hammurabi → Code of 282 laws; Nebuchadnezzar II → Hanging Gardens.
Fix the key dates: Sargon 2334–2279 BCE, Hammurabi 1792–1750 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II 604–562 BCE, Gilgamesh translated 1872 CE.
The Sumerians invented cuneiform; the Babylonians gave the wheel, plough, sundial, 24-hour day, 60-minute hour, and first written laws.
'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth' is Hammurabi's most famous law — punishment should equal the harm.
Distinguish primary sources (artefacts, clay tablets, ruins) from secondary sources (textbooks, biographies).
